E1934.summary: In verses quoted from Norton, the White Stone found through patient labor after true teaching; the white medicine must be fully wrought before the Red is sought.
E1934.body: Norton's verse (quoted, not Atwood's own words) says many patient wise men “Found our White Stone with exercise;” after true teaching, and cautions that the Red should not be sought “Till the white medicine be fully wrought;” [I.1 ¶60]. The White Stone thus apparently marks a stage completed before the red work.

E1935.summary: In Eudoxus's account, the white sulphur separated by whitening the foul black faeces in the first work; identified with the Sal Amoniac of the Wise and their Chaste Diana.
E1935.body: Quoted from Eudoxus: in the first work the foul black faeces are whitened and the white sulphur separated [IV.3 ¶9]. He identifies it as “the white sulphur, which is the Sal Amoniac of the Wise” and as “the Sal Amoniac of the Wise, and their Chaste Diana, who washes herself in the bath” [IV.3 ¶9].

E1936.summary: In a passage from a more modern experimentalist, the white spirit with which the masculine tincture comes out of the black darkness in union.
E1936.body: Quoted from an unnamed “more modern experimentalist” in a footnote: the masculine tincture comes “out of the black darkness together in union with the white virginal spirit” [I.3 n53].

E1937.summary: The stage at which the matter is snow-white and the elixir is perfect as to the white; Norton ties it to making the Moon fortunate.
E1937.body: The author of the Lucerna Salis (quoted) describes the matter become snow-white: “Then is your elixir perfect as to the white work” [III.2 ¶5]; the Latin reads “Et tum confectum est elixir ad album” [III.2 ¶6]. Norton (quoted) directs: “For the white Worke make fortunate the Moone” [IV.2 ¶34]; the text does not explain this further.

E1938.summary: In Sendivogius, the Whites and Reds with which ignorant montebanks deceived almost the whole world.
E1938.body: Sendivogius (quoted) complains of pretenders who “have with their Whites and Reds deceived almost the whole world” [I.1 ¶84]. The expression is not explained there; the context suggests false white and red products of the work.

E1939.summary: In Atwood's own voice, chiefly in the later Appendix, Will is the only true substance and foundation of everything, the binding and unbinding power, and the greatest power of purgation.
E1939.body:
Atwood's own statements; most come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). There she holds that “for Will has substance, nay, is the only substance” and that “it is the Universal Loadstone of Existence” [APP ¶8]; in higher states it moves from its own center, its efflux is chaotic and must be taken up by an external mind [APP ¶8]. “Will creates an image, not a being.”; passing into desire for that image, it unites with it into a being; Will is the only true body [APP ¶36]. “All in the beginning is Will; it is the foundation of everything, and is everything” [APP ¶86]: all is held potentially in it; it subsists in one will, then two, exists in the third, and then becomes self-assertion. “Weight is the analogue of Will.” [APP ¶123]; it binds and unbinds — “that which Will has bound, Will only can unbind” — and is identified with Saturn: “a Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key” [APP ¶125]. Two wills contend for the soul, and vacuity of self-will gives spirits a footing [APP ¶123–125].

In the main text Atwood states that “Will is the greatest power of purgation” [IV.1 ¶31], and that “no mortal can communicate it to another unless the Divine Will be with him” [IV.1 ¶39] — the Divine Will must be conciliated.

E1940.summary: Two separated principles which, once freed, attract one another like steel and loadstone.
E1940.body: Speaker unclear: the text speaks of “the separated principles of Will and Understanding in their freed state” [IV.2 ¶30], which attract each other as steel and loadstone.

E1941.summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's name for the vital power, at a certain time seated in the lumbar region and sent back.
E1941.body: Appendix (later layer), Atwood's voice: “the power, the vital or willing-power” [APP ¶11], at a certain time seated in the lumbar region and sent back.

E1942.summary: In Khunrath, the thick, black substance of the first act, called the Blood of the Earth and identified with the Red of Lully.
E1942.body: Khunrath (quoted) describes it in the first act as “thick, dense, and black, blacker than black” [IV.1 ¶36]. It is “the Wine which the Wise have called the Blood of the Earth”, “which likewise is the Red of Lully” [IV.1 ¶36]; it is called Red for its tincture, the color of its virtue.

E1943.summary: The object of Atwood's inquiry: the ancient internal Wisdom, the true being of Intellect and self-knowledge, identified with Salt, the substance of the Stone, and the Root of Reason.
E1943.body:
Mostly Atwood's own voice. Wisdom is “that Wisdom we are investigating”, identified with Isis and Minerva [III.1 ¶5]; by its Light nature's universal efficient is revealed [III.1 ¶3]. It is the highest faculty: “The term Intellect, as it is here taken in its highest sense, is synonymous with Wisdom” [II.1 ¶39]; “to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul” [II.1 ¶37]; it is “not conversant with a certain definite existing thing but simply with all things” [II.1 ¶37]. Ancient science's theme was “the standard of truth in a rectified intellect”, Wisdom being “an affirmative operative hypostasis, informing, invigorating, and sustaining all things” [II.1 ¶44] and “the offspring of a vital experiment into nature” [II.1 ¶52]. Hermes (as cited) calls it “the good, the fair, and the blessed Eternity” [II.1 ¶43]. It is “not worldly” [II.2 ¶13], intuitive Intellect without imaginative error.

For the method, Atwood ties it to the Stone: Wisdom “was the worthy object of all Hermetic Philosophy, and the miraculous substance of its transmutative Stone”, and “not without weighty cause has Salt been dignified with the name of Wisdom” [III.3 ¶50]; “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20]. From Ecclesiasticus and Solomon (quoted): “For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.” [III.3 ¶49]. It is “the vehicle of the Catholic Reason in Identity, the bearer and measure of the Demiurgic Fire” [III.3 ¶71].

Moral conditions: “No impure leaven (need we repeat it?) can enter into Wisdom” [III.4 ¶7]; the covetous flee “Wisdom’s fiery ordeal” [III.4 ¶11]. “Her secret is with the Faithful” [IV.3 ¶36]; it is given by God “and send thy Holy Spirit from above” [IV.3 ¶39], the gift of perfecting the work [IV.3 ¶48]. It is “a thing acquired, the reward only of peculiar and arduous discipline” [IV.4 ¶17], “above science, art, and every other kind of faith”, the Well of Heraclitus and the Nothing Socrates knew [IV.4 ¶27]; yet “the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared from amongst men” [IV.4 ¶28].

Quoted views: Asclepius Trallianus calls it “a certain clearness” [II.4 ¶26]; Reuchlin: “Nothing is in the beginning but Wisdom, or Sapience”, called Ain by the Hebrews [III.2 ¶10]; the Rabbi says none can tell “in what manner she is contained in non-Being” [III.2 ¶32]. In the Appendix (later layer) it is “a pure exemplar from the first Light or Life, showing man what he ought to be” [APP ¶90], the great Salt Sea or Universal Will [APP ¶94], and the Law of Light's emanating spirit [APP ¶47].

Further asserted identities: Intellect and Divination [II.1 ¶35]; the intelligible essence [II.1 ¶37]; Pythagoras's “science of truth which is in all beings” [II.1 ¶39]; “the breath of the power of God” [II.1 ¶44]; “the fear of the Lord” [III.1 ¶8]; Understanding [IV.3 ¶47]; Reuchlin's Three Persons in Divinity [III.2 ¶10]; the Rabbi's Principle [III.2 ¶32]. With Sendivogius, God inspires his Wisdom into philosophers [II.4 ¶39]; Atwood also personifies her as a bride the philosophers wooed, bringing a dowry of creative light [IV.4 ¶10].

E1944.summary: Anonymous adepts whose unanimous view Atwood reports: that their work may be likened to the creation of the world.
E1944.body: Atwood reports, with approval, the Wise's view that “their work may be likened to the creation of the world” [IV.2 ¶30].

E1945.summary: The adepts as a group, cited by Atwood for their warnings that none succeed without right intention and God's blessing, and that their records are two-edged.
E1945.body: Atwood endorses their declarations that none attain the Art without right intention and God's blessing and that the pursuit is dangerous to the ill-informed: “As the adepts indeed foretold, their records have proved like a curious two-edged instrument” [III.4 ¶11, III.4 ¶16].

E1946.summary: An unnamed adept cited as warning that Pluto's Palace exposed with Minerva's Artifice, or Vulcan with her at the Altar, is an ominous association.
E1946.body: Cited by Atwood: when Pluto's Palace is exposed with Minerva's Artifice, or Vulcan stands with her at the Altar, “the Association is ominous” [IV.1 ¶34].

E1947.summary: The adepts whose enigmas, fables, parables and maxims, Atwood says, all tend to one discovery and must be studied with the Key.
E1947.body: Atwood, with approval, says their enigmas, fables, parables and maxims all tend to one discovery and are to be studied with the Key [IV.4 ¶32].

E1948.summary: In Eudoxus, the operator who lends Nature a hand for her compound and himself makes the compound of Art.
E1948.body: Eudoxus (quoted): Nature's compound is helped by the Artist, but of the compound of Art “it is always the Artist who makes it”, “it is the Wise man who makes it” [IV.3 ¶9].

forms: the wise poet, in his Georgics
E1949.summary: An unnamed poet whose Georgics Atwood cites for the repeated labor of ploughing and clearing the field.
E1949.body: Cited by Atwood for teaching, in the Georgics, the repeated labor of ploughing and clearing the field [IV.1 ¶9]; the context suggests an image for the repeated operations of the work.

E1950.summary: In the Poemander of Hermes, the holy Word issuing from the Light or Mind, joining itself to Nature and moving the elements; the Son of God.
E1950.body: Hermes (Poemander, quoted): “Then from that Light a certain holy Word joined itself unto Nature” [III.3 ¶53], drawing the fire upward and moving earth and water; “that bright and lightful Word from the Mind is the Son of God” [III.3 ¶54]. God's Will took it in making the world.

E1951.summary: What, Atwood says, the ancestors sought and experimentally found through subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects.
E1951.body: Atwood: “the Word of Life would seem to have been sought after by our ancestors, and experimentally found” [IV.2 ¶43], by subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects.

E1952.summary: In the Appendix, words by which the Initiated moved one another on, found only in the subjective life and lost by the Masons.
E1952.body: Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “The Initiated moved one another on by words of power.”; these are words “which are only to be found by seeking them in the subjective, the fundamental life” [APP ¶100]. The Masons have lost them.

E1953.summary: In Eudoxus, the three closely analogous works of the Art, each repeating dissolution, removal of blackness, whitening and vivifying.
E1953.body: Eudoxus (quoted): “the operations of the three works have a great deal of analogy one to another” [IV.3 ¶3]; each repeats dissolution, removal of blackness, whitening and vivifying, and the philosophers deliberately confuse them.

E1954.summary: In the theosophist's teaching, one of two principles in everything, predominant in outward nature since the fall and to be subdued as servant to the light.
E1954.body: The theosophist (quoted): every thing has two principles, of which the wrath fire has predominated in outward nature since the fall and must be subdued to serve the light. “The serpent’s sting is the wrath fire” [IV.3 ¶38].

E1955.summary: Writers whom Atwood credits with rightly linking Trance to the temple mysteries but faults for going no further than therapy.
E1955.body: Atwood qualifies them: they rightly connect Trance with the temple mysteries but do not go beyond its therapeutic use [II.2 ¶6].

E1956.summary: Reported through Aristotle as first to introduce the doctrine that the One is God, and dismissed there as rustic.
E1956.body: As reported via Aristotle, Xenophanes first introduced the doctrine that “the One is God” and was dismissed as rustic [III.2 ¶40].

E1957.summary: Author of an Opusculum whom Atwood cites on long searching for the key, on prayer before the Work, and on one method, matter and vessel.
E1957.body: Atwood cites Zachary's Opusculum as another example of long searching for the key [III.1 ¶37, III.1 n42]. With approval, she cites him that one should read the philosophers and pray, yet use means: “for no one ever acquired this art by chance, but by prayer rather than by other means” [III.4 ¶20, III.4 n17]. Against many furnaces and vessels: “there is indeed but one way of working, in one matter, one linear way throughout” [IV.1 ¶9, IV.1 n12].

E1958.summary: Cited by Atwood for the ether as plastic, generating fire, and, within Vaughan's lessons, for listening much and speaking little.
E1958.body: Atwood cites Zeno for the ether as an artful generating fire: “Ignem esse artificiosum, ad gignendum progredientem via” [I.2 ¶16] (ours: that fire is artful, proceeding methodically to generate). Within Vaughan's lessons he is quoted: “Nature gave us one tongue and two ears, that we might hear much and speak little” [III.4 ¶44].

E1959.summary: Cited by Atwood in support of the absolute unit as the ground of Being.
E1959.body: Atwood cites him in support: “if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being” [III.2 ¶45].

E1960.summary: A work Atwood cites on the formless Divinity, the Initial Principle as Wisdom manifesting by a point of Light, and the celestial prototype in humanity.
E1960.body: Atwood cites the Zohar in support: Divinity has no form before descent into creation, so no image may represent Him [II.3 ¶48, II.3 n52]; the Initial Principle is Wisdom or the Supreme Crown, the Unknown who manifests — “he begins by producing a point” — with its white appearance [III.2 ¶3, III.2 n3, III.2 n4]. The Liber Zohar “beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity” and shows the covert fire in Holy Writ [II.1 ¶40].

E1962.summary: Cited by Atwood for magic as the service of the gods, for the Prester as Fire Spirit of Life, and for the ladder reaching from Tartarus to Heaven.
E1962.body: His magic is described as the service of the gods [II.1 ¶51]. Atwood identifies with the Stone or Salt “the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life” [II.3 ¶54]. She identifies with the magnetic chain “that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54].

E1963.summary: Oracles used as a chapter epigraph exhorting the reader to the Light.
E1963.body: Used as the chapter epigraph: “It behooves thee to hasten to the Light, and to the beams of the Father” [II.4 ¶2].

E1964.summary: An Egyptian reputed a great practitioner, named among authors of extant treatises on the philosophers' stone.
E1964.body: Named as an Egyptian reputed a great practitioner [I.1 ¶29], and listed with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras and Archelaus among authors of extant treatises on the stone [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34].
